doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Church, energy and the state of jazz
title: Sonny Rollins's Harlem reunion concert and being called a relic
summary: Rollins's concert reunites old Harlem neighbours like Percy Heath and Gil Coggins; Cranshaw says older players are pushed aside as relics.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And they’re gone. Which is nice because it gives other people a chance to work off of their situations, but we don’t get to hear the great ones and what they were doing. Tomorrow or Saturday there’s a Sonny Rollins concert and he’s using, on the concert, his, a group of people who grew up in Harlem in a certain neighborhood. The only one, Art Taylor died, so he would ordinarily have been the drummer. But Percy Heath and he’s using Gil Coggins, one of the piano players that’s worked, what do they call themselves, I forget the part of Harlem, but they live 150s up in there. But they were all neighbors. And Jackie McLean and Sonny Rollins, all of these people, as young guys, played together or experienced different things at the same time, together. So they’re kind of a reenactment of, and Walter Bishop, and some of them are going to be on the show. I don’t know what they’re going to play, I’m not sure what is going to happen yet. But it’s a joy just to see that group together. There’s some energy in the air. A lot of them haven’t played or don’t play a lot, but it’s just nice to see it, you know. There’s something about that kind of professionalism that I think that more young people should see. But we don’t have the chance to see it because the older guys kind of are already moved to the side as relics. We only read about the older guys. Bob Cranshaw, I’ll be 63, I’m a relic already.
